title: Lynx reintroduction from a bottlenecked source exposes a lethal genetic defect - Nature Ecology & Evolution
byline: Niehaus; Janna; Imlau; Michelle; Keller; Saskia; Marti; Iris; Breitenmoser; Christine; Letko; Jagannathan; Vidhya; Hiller; Lea Anna; Naguleswaran; Arunasalam; R
html:
Abstract

Conservation programmes worldwide use reintroductions and translocations as management tools to support endangered species. However, such efforts often result in small and isolated populations that face genetic challenges associated with reduced gene flow and inbreeding. Inbreeding depression is a well-known risk in such programmes, as increased homozygosity can expose recessive deleterious alleles, compromise fitness and threaten population persistence. Yet, no causal variant for a lethal disease has previously been identified in a wild population. Here we combine long-term health and population data with genomic analyses to identify a recessive loss-of-function allele causing lethal organ mineralization in young Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) from a reintroduced population in Switzerland. Spatio-temporal analyses revealed that the allele was introduced from one of the source populations and increased in frequency through founder effects and inbreeding. Our findings establish the first direct link between reintroduction history and a lethal genetic disease in the wild, illustrating how population genetic processes interact to shape the fate of a recessive deleterious allele and emphasize the vulnerability of small, isolated populations following reintroduction.

Main

Every species reintroduction is not only an ecological intervention but also an inadvertent experiment in evolutionary genetics. Reintroductions are a widely used conservation strategy to prevent extinction, yet they carry important genetic risks. Bottlenecks and small founder populations typical of reintroductions not only lead to loss of genetic diversity and thereby loss of adaptive potential, they can also accelerate the accumulation of harmful mutations, posing an additional risk to fitness and threatening long-term viability1. The role of deleterious mutations for survival of wild populations and how this should affect management decisions of endangered species is a central question for ongoing research. Recent studies have evaluated genome-wide estimates of putatively harmful mutations as a consequence of small population size2,3,4,5,6. Yet while population genetic models consistently predict substantial risks from such mutations7, empirical examples from wild populations linking deleterious mutations with fitness declines remain scarce8,9,10. To date, no lethal disease in a wild population has been causally linked to a specific genetic variant.

Inbreeding depression, which mainly arises through expression of harmful recessive alleles, has been associated with reduced reproductive output, lower juvenile survival, compromised immunity, shortened lifespans and population viability8,9,11,12,13,14,15. However, few studies bridge the gap between specific genomic evidence and phenotypic consequences. Beyond genome-wide measures of inbreeding and mutational load, individual genetic variants have been shown to substantially influence phenotypic variation with consequences for reproductive success and adaptation, hence secondarily affecting individual fitness and survival16,17,18. In a wild population of the primitive domestic Soay sheep, variation within RXFP2 was shown to be linked to horn growth and survival resulting in heterozygote advantage19. In the small and isolated Similipal tiger population an LVRN missense variant was identified as the basis of a pseudomelanistic phenotype20. Although no fitness effects have been detected, the tiger example illustrates how genetic drift can lead to the spread of novel traits in inbred populations. Such findings highlight the importance of monitoring genetic processes in small, isolated and reintroduced populations.

The reintroduction of the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) in Switzerland provides a unique opportunity to study the long-term genetic consequences of conservation management actions. Once extirpated from central Europe, the species was re-established in the 1970s through the translocation of about 30 lynx from the Carpathians into the Swiss Alps and Jura Mountains21,22. Since then, the total number of Swiss lynx has grown to roughly 360 individuals23 and has been continuously monitored for over 50 years. Despite this increase in population size, genetic diversity has been severely reduced, with observed heterozygosity approximately 30% lower than in the Carpathian source population21,24. Thirty years after the reintroduction, the Alpine and Jura populations remained largely isolated. To improve connectivity and enhance the lynx distribution, between 2001 and 2008 a total of 12 animals were captured from the two existing populations (4 females and 4 males from the Alps population; 3 females and 1 male from the Jura Mountains population) and translocated to a territory between them in northeastern Switzerland (Fig. 1). Of these, only 7 individuals (3 females and 1 male from the Alps population; 1 female and 2 males from the Jura population) were ultimately confirmed to have contributed to the establishment of the new population (NE-CH)25, and gene flow among the three regions remains limited, resulting in persistently low genetic diversity24. Complementing demographic and genetic data, Switzerland has implemented intensive health surveillance on the lynx populations, which has revealed that several young lynx from the NE-CH population are exhibiting severe and ultimately lethal soft-tissue mineralization.

The combined comprehensive data gave us the opportunity to close the current gap between genetics and phenotypic consequences in an inbred wildlife population. We show how reintroduction bottlenecks, founder effects and subsequent inbreeding can lead to the manifestation of a lethal recessive allele in a wild population, providing an empirical example of the evolutionary risks associated with conservation actions.

Results

Regional clustering of fatal multi-organ mineralization in young Eurasian lynx

The Eurasian lynx is a protected species in Switzerland, and therefore post-mortem examinations of all lynx that are (1) found dead, (2) euthanized due to health issues or (3) culled due to repeated livestock predation are part of the national implementation guidelines26 (see also ref. 27). All post-mortem examinations are carried out at the Institute for Fish and Wildlife Health. Since the 1980s bio-banking of biological samples has been conducted, and since 2000, health findings have systematically been recorded in a dedicated database. To investigate the occurrence of the mineralization phenotype in more detail, a retrospective case review (2000–2023), including histopathological reassessment, was performed. The search of the database comprising 421 entries resulted in 13 lynx with reported multifocal mineralization. The histological reassessment of these animals revealed nine cases that exhibited a very uniform mineralization pattern affecting kidney, lung and stomach and were found between the years 2012–2022 (Supplementary Table 1). Four animals, which exhibited only a mild and markedly different pattern of mineralization, were excluded from further investigation. Six of the identified cases were found dead and three were found weak and emaciated. Of the latter, one was euthanized and the other two died shortly after being found. The affected individuals were all young (juvenile or subadult following ref. 28), of equal sex ratio and found in the northeastern part of Switzerland (NE-CH). On histopathology, affected animals exhibited diffuse marked mineralization in the renal cortex (Fig. 2a,d), lung (Fig. 2b,e) and gastric mucosal layer (Fig. 2c,f), consistent with metastatic mineralization. In all animals, the severity of these organ lesions was deemed incompatible with normal organ function and considered ultimately fatal. A detailed overview of the pathological findings and case background is compiled in Supplementary Table 1).

a–f, Representative serial sections of kidney (a,d), lung (b,e) and stomach (c,f) from an affected lynx stained with H&E (a–c) and von Kossa stain (d–f). Mineralization is visible as dark purple crystalline structures in H&E sections and as black colouration in von Kossa stain. g–l, Corresponding sections from a non-affected lynx are shown, with kidney (g,j), lung (h,k) and stomach (i,l) stained with H&E (g–i) and von Kossa stain (j–l).

Strong population differentiation and high levels of inbreeding

Given the very small number of founders of the affected NE-CH population (Fig. 1), together with the early age of disease onset and the clustered origin of affected individuals, a heritable disease caused by a deleterious recessive allele and inbreeding was suspected. We therefore subjected the 9 mineralization cases from the NE-CH population and 41 controls from all three Swiss lynx populations (Alps = 20, Jura = 13, NE-CH = 8; Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2) to short-read whole-genome sequencing. A principal component analysis (PCA) on 1,899,640 high‑quality biallelic autosomal variants (Supplementary Table 3) recapitulated the geographic population structure (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 2), which was confirmed by STRUCTURE-like analysis (Extended Data Fig. 3). The nine affected individuals were nested within the NE-CH population, with no separation of cases from controls (Fig. 3a).

a, PCA plot of the first two principal components (PC1 versus PC2), demonstrating clear genetic separation among all three Swiss lynx populations. The nine mineralization cases are clustered exclusively within the NE-CH population. b, Boxplots of individual FROH values (proportion of the genome in ROHs >1 Mb) for each population, highlighting high inbreeding levels across all populations. Each jittered point represents one independently sampled individual. c, Distribution of ROH lengths >10 Mb across the three populations. Each jittered point represents one ROH segment >10 Mb. See also Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5. For all plots sample sizes were as follows: Alps, n = 20; Jura, n = 13; and NE-CH, n = 17. Boxplots show the median (centre line), interquartile range (box) and whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5× the interquartile range.

Runs of homozygosity (ROH) analysis across the autosomal genome confirmed very high levels of inbreeding in all three lynx populations, consistent with mating among siblings and between parents and offspring (Fig. 3b,c). The Alpine population exhibited the highest levels of inbreeding, the Jura population showed the lowest, and the NE-CH population displayed intermediate levels of inbreeding and a wider range of inbreeding coefficient based on ROH (FROH) values (proportion of genome within ROH larger than 1 Mb), reflecting heterogeneous inbreeding patterns (Fig. 3b, more details in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). Analyses of particularly long ROH segments (>10 Mb, indicative of recent inbreeding) showed the highest levels in the NE-CH population, consistent with its more recent reintroduction history and a very small number of founders (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5).

Identification of the causal variant for the lethal mineralization phenotype

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) using a further reduced dataset comprising 1,699,701 high‑quality markers yielded a strong association signal (P = 4.88 × 10−8) on scaffold NW_025814889.1 at position 39,312,590 (Fig. 4a,b). All nine cases were homozygous at the best associated marker, supporting an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

a, Manhattan plot visualizing the association between genetic variants and the phenotypic trait. P values were calculated using a linear mixed model (Methods). The x axis represents genome positions grouped by scaffolds and the y axis indicates the −log10(P) for each variant. Genome-wide significance and suggestive significance thresholds were calculated using the Bonferroni correction for multiple testing, based on 1,699,701 independent variants tested (P = 0.05/1,699,701 = 2.93 × 10−8 for genome-wide significance, marked by the red dashed line; and P = 1.0/1,699,701 = 5.88 × 10−7 for suggestive significance, marked by the black dashed line). One variant exceeded the suggestive significance threshold (P = 4.88 × 10−8) on scaffold NW_025814889.1. b, Quantile–quantile plot comparing the observed distribution of −log10(P) with the expected distribution under the null hypothesis (no association, red line). c, Details of the p.L13P variant. The signal peptides of the lynx and human FGF23 precursor proteins are highlighted in yellow and amino acids identical for the two species are shown in between. The position of the lynx p.L13P variant and the cleavage site are indicated by arrows. d, Experimental validation of defective secretion of the mutant protein. HEK293 cells were transfected with expression constructs encoding wild-type and mutant lynx signal peptides fused to the human FGF23 mature protein, or were left untransfected as negative controls. Expression of the protein was assessed in the cell pellet (left), whereas secretion was examined in the culture supernatants (centre). A distinct band corresponding to the secreted protein was detected only in the culture supernatant of cells expressing the wild-type (wt) signal peptide fused to FGF23, whereas no corresponding band was observed for the mutant (L13P) protein, indicating impaired secretion. The loading control (right) confirmed comparable protein loading between samples. This experiment was repeated twice independently with similar results.

Filtering of all originally identified 17,328,023 raw variants (Supplementary Table 3) for homozygous alternate genotypes exclusively in the nine cases but in none of the controls identified one single position, which corresponded to the best associated variant in the GWAS and was located within a ROH in all nine affected individuals (Extended Data Fig. 6). The identified variant, NW_025814889.1:g.39,312,590A>G, corresponds to a missense variant in the FGF23 gene encoding fibroblast growth factor 23, XM_047065192.1:c.38T>C. It is predicted to change leucine-13 in the signal peptide of the FGF23 protein into a proline, XP_046921148.1:p.(Leu13Pro) (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8).

FGF23 is a key regulator of phosphorous homeostasis and negatively regulates matrix mineralization through a variety of pathways and interactions29. In humans, various FGF23 loss-of-function alleles cause familial tumoral calcinosis, which presents as soft-tissue hypermineralization30. FGF23 activity is heavily regulated at the protein level. Removal of an N-terminal signal peptide is required for export and activity, while cleavage of a C-terminal fragment terminates activity31. Although the p.Leu13Pro variant uncovered in the Swiss lynx population is not homologous to any of the disease variants identified in humans30, several complementary computational methods predicted it to be pathogenic or have a disease-causing effect, most likely due to defective recognition and cleavage of the signal peptide (Supplementary Note 2 and Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8). Next, in vitro expression of recombinant constructs encoding the wild-type or mutant lynx signal peptide fused to the human mature FGF23 protein was performed. This experiment confirmed that only the wild-type lynx signal peptide mediates secretion, while the mutant protein was retained within the transfected cells (Fig. 4c,d).
